newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch rail privatisation speeds ahead of politics.
newsitem.headline: Dutch rail privatisation speeds ahead of politics.

text.p: Two transport companies emerged on Monday as candidates to bid for Dutch rail services and others were said to be queuing up, although the Transport Ministry has yet to finish setting the guidelines on competition.

Regional transport companies Hermes and Vancom are keen to take over loss-making regional train services from Dutch Railways, saying they could do a better and cheaper job than the state-owned monopoly.
The Dutch government currently pays 130 million guilders ($78.50 million) a year to the national railway company as compensation for keeping loss-making lines in service.
The state aims to cut back the subsidies and liberalise the train market and is still studying ways to introduce competition in passenger traffic.
But it has been taken over by events as the first private Dutch rail company, Lovers Rail, began a succesful beach-service between Amsterdam and sea-resort IJmuiden in August.

State-owned Hermes and Vancom Nederland, a unit of Oakbrook Terrace, Illinois-based transport group Vancom Inc, now also want a slice of the rail market and have urged Transport Minister Annemarie Jorritsma to take a decision.

"They are moving too slow. The politicians aren't clear what they want with train services and whether they want to open a public bidding for the loss-making regional train services," said Vancom's supervisory board chairman Kees Arends.

Vancom was the first private transporter in the Netherlands when it began public bus services in 1995 in the southern Dutch province of Limburg and the northern province of Groningen. It is now interested in running trains in the same two regions.

Vancom will offer a deal similar to one in 1994 when it won bus lines from state-owned companies such as Hermes by offering 30 percent more services against the same amount of government subsidies, Arends said.
Although beaten by Vancom once, Limburg-based Hermes is confident it could offer a competitive deal for three regional train services in Limburg.

"We will transform these three train services into cheaper light-rail trains and weave them into our bus lines. We also intend to extend the tracks into the cities. That should get us more passengers," a spokesman said.
"If we do all that, we can do it much cheaper than Dutch Railways," he added.

Ticket revenues cover only 54 percent of the costs of regional train services. Regional bus and tram companies do an even worse job with 45-50 percent coverage of costs, but total costs of these companies are smaller.
Meanwhile, Dutch Railways has not given up on its 30 loss-making regional train services and intends to take part in the public bidding that is due to open later this year.

"Dutch Railways would like continue running trains in the regions, but the state will always have to put money on top. Even if the services are run by others such as Hermes or Vancom," spokesman Tijs Manten said.
Meanwhile, cargo rail services are also being liberalised and several transport companies were preparing a launch, said head of capacity allocation at rail manager Railned, Ben Bras.

"Cargo services are easier to liberalise than passenger services for which you need a licence. A cargo company just needs to be acknowledged as a transporter and can then start submitting requests for time slots," he said.
Among the cargo companies interested in running their own trains across Europe were large Rotterdam-based transporters, he said. These could include Nedlloyd and Van Ommeren.
